utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Shall we go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we resume hearing the evidence, it's about the court schedule of 16th of June, which is Thursday, next week. On 16th of June, in the morning, the extraordinary Judges' Plenary -- or regular Judges' Plenary is scheduled to take place in the morning, so evidently we are not able to sit. So my suggestion is that we sit for three days in that week and instead to sit five days in the following week, i.e., to sit on 24th of June, Friday, if that does not cause a lot of problems to the parties. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd have to, if the Court permits, at least take a few moments to consider that against the scheduling of witnesses. I'm sure that's what in part what the Court would like us -- to know and need a little time to consider the implications.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So if the parties could let the Chamber know during the course of today if there's any problem. Then let's bring in Mr. Neskovic. My understanding is that, Mr. Karadzic, you have about an hour and a half to conclude your cross-examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Yes, Excellency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Neskovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karadzic, please continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency. Good morning to one and all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to you, too, Mr. Neskovic.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We left off yesterday discussing the incidents and crimes which took place, and you expressed -- you're sorry that these crimes weren't prosecuted. Now, were you informed -- did you receive a follow-up? Were you informed about what was going on -- what happened to the perpetrators of those crimes?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I have to remind you to make pauses between question and answer to facilitate the work of our interpreters, who become very tired. Now, it's possible that justice was slow in coming but came nonetheless without you having been given feedback information?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm afraid that the police organs and the courts didn't work as they should have done during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you mean to say that they didn't exist?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they did exist. They were fully organised. There was civilians control, the civilian police force, civilian courts, military security, the military police, military prosecutor's offices, and military courts. So they were fully constituted. However, they didn't prosecute, they didn't do very much. Now, why? I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But they might have been doing their job without you knowing about it?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, I don't think so, because had they been doing their job Batko would have been arrested, an indictment raised against him and a lawsuit taken against him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, were you at Grbavica at the beginning of August 1992?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When did you leave Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In April 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember, or rather, do you know where Lenin Street number 2 is?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what part of Grbavica is that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's Grbavica 1, in the centre of town, a long street, in the centre of Grbavica, one of the main streets branching off from Zagrebacka Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And our authority was established there somewhere towards the end of May, right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we were in a facility called Mis and this facility was in Zagrebacka Street and formerly it was a department store. After being a department store it was a bank and now it's been destroyed. We came there from Vrace when the Serb army placed Grbavica under its control. I think that was around the 10th of May, but I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember a drastic event that took place on the 3rd of August, 1992, when a Serb entered the basement with a rifle and killed Husein Dobric and another citizen Borislav, I don't know whether he was a Serb or a Croat, this other man Borislav, but anyway it took place in the basement of the building in Lenin Street number 2?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Judging by the first name and surname, this man, Husein, was he a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, judging by his name I would say he was a Bosniak, a Muslim, as his first name is Husein.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, do you know what happened to the perpetrator whose name was Jovo Pejanovic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we now have D596 displayed, please, on e-court, yes. D596 is the document number. And may we have the translation placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this a document of the military court in Sarajevo written on the 17th of December, 1992?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this a judgement by which the accused, Jovo Pejanovic, is being sentenced and said to be guilty because on the 3rd of August, 1992, at about 2300 hours, he entered -- stormed into Lenin Street -- well, you read the paragraph to yourself.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the judgement?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Why he has been found guilty?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have only three lines there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we scroll down. The verdict. That's right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you then agree -- well, it says why he was found guilty, because on the 3rd of August he went into the basement of the building and killed these two people; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we turn to the next page in Serbian and probably in English too. Next page, please. Unfortunately we don't have that part in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that it says that he has been given a prison sentence of ten years and the prison sentence is counted -- the time spent in detention from the 4th of August, 1992, is counted as running. Now, do you agree that on the 3rd of August, the man committed the crime; and on the 4th of August, he was already arrested and sentenced and found guilty and kept in prison for the next ten years? Thank you --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm sorry that this hasn't been translated, but as it's a Prosecution document, we would like to have the whole verdict and judgement translated with the statement of reasons because it was a drastic event and it was prosecuted and there was a trial and there was a solution, but you didn't know about that. So I ask you again: Did things happen which you didn't know about?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course. Military affairs, police affairs, security affairs were realms that I knew nothing about. I wasn't informed about them and I didn't deal with anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let's go back to the Batko case --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And may I have 65 ter 52 -- 5268, please, P5268 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we proceed, I'm just wondering why this document has been admitted without being marked for identification, given there is no English translation. E-court says "English translation to be uploaded." So I wonder whether it's too late to mark this for identification until we have the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we admitted it under the expectation that the hard copy used at the time would be uploaded immediately, but that didn't take place. Do we have a full translation in hard copy?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We received this part of the translation from the Prosecution and we thought it was the entire translation, but now we see that it isn't. So we'll have to translate the rest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Knowing that, we'll mark it for identification until we have the full translation. Very well. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We needn't keep it on the ELMO any longer. May we have P2568, page 115 first and then we're going on to 116.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect to the last document, if I could just note for the record that was belatedly disclosed. I don't have an issue with that. The Defence advised me of that, but that just came to our attention this morning just before coming into court. I only note that because for a couple of reasons, number one, these things do happen but it's probably best to note when they do and an accommodation -- or no objection is made by the other party; and number two, it may implicate the Prosecution's ability to address it at this moment rather than later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That has been noted. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Defence is grateful for Mr. Tieger's understanding, but this emerged from a sentence uttered by the witness yesterday. Now, may we have line 24 and 25 of this page displayed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger asked you here, he said: [In English] "Mr. Neskovic, you mentioned someone named Batko. First of all, do you know whether he -- he held any official position within the military police or any other body?" [Interpretation] And your answer: [In English] "No. He was an armed monster, a pathological type." [Interpretation] Do you stand by the fact that he had no official position and that he was as you described him?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but he must have been a member of some unit, I don't know which.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was he a member of a military or paramilitary unit?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as to paramilitary units, I don't know about them being in Grbavica. They couldn't have survived. I think they all had to be tied to the army in one way or another.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, let's take a look at the following page -- we are on that page. Staying with this page then. [In English] "He wore an army uniform and nothing more than that. And I don't know whether he was a member of a paramilitary unit or a regular army unit; I really don't know. I don't know what the make-up of those military formations were. But he did a lot of bad things there. Because with mutual efforts on the part of both Serbs and Muslims, we managed to more or less strike a balance, and then an individual like that comes along and acts like a monster, and he spoils everything. And I mean, during the day, there were police officers there, and later on we had the French army there, and the security situation was rather good. But at night we had a problem because there was no lighting; there was no electricity; it's a big town, and the front lines were crossing across town." [Interpretation] And so on and so forth. And line 18: [In English] "So whenever you crossed him in the streets, you didn't know whether he was going to say hello to you or he was going to shoot you ..." [Interpretation] Now, from this does it follow that Batko chose a night when the police and the citizens and the authorities weren't able to follow him and prevent him from doing what he did?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't an eye-witness of his crimes, but the night when -- but at night security was nil.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is the following correct, that instead of saying hello he might shoot you and that you were never quite sure which he would do?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Serbs avoided him and the Bosniaks and Croats shuddered when they heard his name mentioned every day.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we now have the next page displayed, please, page 116. Next page, 16703.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English] "And we went to Simo Sipcic, who was the head of the police at the time, and then he ran to some -- Batko's rooms, and he saved Orhan Djipa and the dog. So Simo could interfere -- or rather, could intervene with his cousin that this person should be taken away or imprisoned or sent away. And we wanted to free Grbavica from this guy, but then somehow after two or three weeks he would always come back. He kept coming back, and then he would once again ask for this person to be removed ..." [Interpretation] And below line 12: [In English] "I think even Biljana Plavsic intervened once and asked for him to be removed from the area once ..." and so on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 118 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While we're waiting, when you talk about Simo Sipcic and when you say that with the help of his relative he could have removed him, you're talking about General Sipcic who was corps commander at the time?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Sipcic was, I think, chief of the military police and he was an example of a person in the security organs who tried to do something about it. Others were rather passive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In line 11: [In English] "Was it understood that the primary targets of his attacks were Muslims and Croats?" [Interpretation] Your answer: [In English] "To some extent, yes, but the main targets of his attacks always had to do with money and looting, and then, of course, especially Muslims and Croats. Mostly Muslims ..." [Interpretation] Is it then the case that Serbs feared him too, as you said a moment ago? Was it easy to arrest him?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the military intelligence service had planned an operation to arrest him even if they had to kill him, and that's the reason why he ran away?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an another example when a person was picked up the next day after the crime. Batko, on the contrary, was committing crimes for a long time, over a period; and the military security organs were certainly able to arrest him. They had the capacity. They had the ability to prosecute him and try him, just like in the case that you yourself mentioned a moment ago --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, because the answer was overlapping with your question or the previous answer was not clear to which question it was given. You answered "yes," Mr. Neskovic, to the question whether it was then the case that Serbs feared him as well, as you said a moment ago. But what was your answer to the question -- to the next question of the accused, asking whether it was easy to arrest him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So it was easy to arrest him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The military police had the force, had the legal authority, as did the military prosecutor's office. They could have arrested him any time they liked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you don't know that that operation had been planned, and that's the reason why he ran, when he noticed they were encircling him?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, Mr. Karadzic. He didn't terrorise the population for just one day; he did that for months. I don't know about that planned operation for his arrest.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did he have protection from anyone in the authorities, from you?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, certainly not from anyone in the Crisis Staff. We had no contact with him. Now, whether he had protection from someone in the security organs or some other organs, I don't know, maybe.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we look at page 123.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would his gang have opposed his arrest, taking up arms?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. The commander of his group was a well-known fighting man, Zoran Zivkovic, who later died from his wounds. And I don't think his group would have tried to obstruct his arrest.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Look at page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Judge. [In English] "The witness is meant to answer this question; that is to say, how does he explain the fact that when faced with actions carried out by this gentleman, Batko, and others, he did not decide to alert the highest civilian or military authorities, for that matter, especially considering that he had the possibility of contacting them on the basis of his position." [Interpretation] Answer. [In English] "As to my own situation, I informed the chief of military police because I knew him in person. It was Mr. Sipcic. The higher-ranking officials at Pale had not been informed. I did not inform them because I thought that it was up to the civilian population, the State Security Services ..." [Interpretation] And so on. And from line 18: [In English] "As to my civic duty to raise the issue of Batko at the Crisis Staff or of opposing Batko openly, we did not dare do that because we would have lost our lives, quite simply, because apart from all the other obligations, we also had a duty to protect our own lives and those of our families." [Interpretation] Did you state that in your testimony in the Krajisnik case and does this reflect reality?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the next page, 124.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: From line 8: [In English] "And also, you've heard the fact that the top leadership at Pale was told about Batko by Biljana Plavsic and it never yielded any results, and that meant that the civilian authorities were not in a position to prevent crimes unless they are in command of the military and police forces, as well ..." [Interpretation] Do you agree and do you remember that in Grbavica, in the municipality, the president of the Executive Board, Budo Obradovic, a well-respected man, was killed?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember he was killed by an armed Serb?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was some settlement of accounts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was it then difficult to protect the life of the man number one in the municipality under those circumstances in Grbavica? He was killed because they failed to protect him.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult to protect the life of an individual at any given moment in war, but it's also a fact that security organs, both civilian and the military, could have done more to protect the lives of the population, Serbs, Croats, and Muslims alike. They had the capacity, they had the force, they had legal authority. They could have applied them. They could have done much more.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you personally also afraid? Is that the reason why you went to your friend and colleague Orhan Djipa, to protect him but also to hide yourself?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to Orhan Djipa to give him the little help I could. It was in an apartment owned by a Serb woman, Mrs. Varagic, on the day when the Muslims were being expelled to the other side from Grbavica. They were in the apartment of Olja Varagic, sitting there together, and they were afraid, not knowing what to do if a group came to their door to drive them out. So we sat down together and made a sort of plan. If somebody comes I would answer the door and say that I lived there. It was not much of a plan, just luckily nobody came to the door that day, none of those people who were driving out Muslims and making them go to the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say you couldn't have given those people any orders. You were just going to say it was your apartment?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I couldn't have given any orders to anyone. I had no authority vis-à-vis the military or the police. And otherwise, the military had a certain hostility to the civilian authorities in Grbavica. There was a day when they practically kidnapped us from the municipality building, put us in trucks, and took us to the front line, said that we were an anti-terrorist unit, we had no right to go home, pick up any clothes, and tell our families. In this very crude manner, everyone from the municipality was just packed into trucks and taken to the front line. So the attitude of the military to the Crisis Staff was completely lacking in respect. It was even hostile because the army people thought that in an area affected by combat, only the military can rule, not civilian authorities. We thought otherwise. We thought that war zone is also a zone of residence. Anyway, the military authorities had no respect or recognition for us and we certainly couldn't order them to do anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Since you were part of the organs of the Serbian Democratic Party from the day it was founded until the end of the war, you were in the leadership, in the Executive Board, was there ever a moment when you realised that the SDS was developing a policy according to which Muslims should be expelled in -- from Serb-populated territories?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the Main Board is concerned and its conclusions, the answer is no. The same answer applies to the Executive Board, but what individual officials did in individual municipalities, we would have to look at that case by case. I don't know about that. I believe that things differed a lot from municipality to municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you have any knowledge that I, myself, wish or are suggesting or am advising to anyone that Croats and Muslims should be expelled from the territories where we were the majority?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't heard it, but in the A and B document it says that Muslims and Croats would not be expelled but Serbian authority would be applied to them. They would be made to submit to Serb authority and that they would later be made to get involved and join the Serbian authority. So the Variant A and B document does not envisage their expulsion, but their submission to Serb authority in some municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It is the position of the Defence that that document, A and B, was received from well-intentioned retired officers. I'm asking you about that document. Have I ever expressed the desire through the SDS that we wished to get rid of Muslims and Croats?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First there are two questions in your question. That document, first of all, was not written by well-intentioned officers. I believe it was a trick played upon the SDS by that group of officers, that's one; and second, your attitude toward Croats and Muslims was that they should be kept at any cost within Yugoslavia because you were hung-up on the Yugoslav issue first and foremost and the Serb issue came second on your agenda, and you wanted Muslims and Croats to stay within Yugoslavia. That was the primary objective of your policy, to keep Bosnia, including Muslims and Croats, within Yugoslavia; however, their legitimate wish and will was different - they wanted to secede.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you understand the policy of the Serbian Democratic Party at any point as wishing or advising or suggesting that Muslims and Croats should be beaten, mistreated, or killed?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The Serbian Democratic Party spent all its efforts on the hopeless Yugoslav issue, trying to keep together a state that had already dissolved, and that applies to all the leadership. The SDS did not have as its priority the Yugoslav or even the Serb issue -- sorry, did not have as its priority the Muslim or Croat or even Serb issue, just the Yugoslav issue. That's why there were these negotiations with Izetbegovic, where you even offered him the Presidency of Yugoslavia if they agreed to stay. This preservation of Yugoslavia was your primary interest, and Serbian and other interests took second place. Your policy towards Muslims and Croats, therefore, was to keep them within Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But once it was obvious that Yugoslavia could not survive, have you ever noticed that the SDS had a programme aimed at destroying Muslims and Croats as ethnic groups? Did such a culture, such an idea, ever exist? Has it ever been built into the programme of the SDS to expel or destroy these two ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the level of the programme of the Main Board and Executive Board, absolutely no. At the level of municipal boards, I don't know, I can't say. All I can talk about is the Novo Sarajevo municipality which I know about, but I can't say what local officials did in the various municipalities and how far they abused their power and authority. But from the view of party programmes and so on, no, there wasn't this hostile attitude at all towards the Bosniaks and Croats in the sense of persecution. But it was thought that everything should be done for the Bosniaks and Croats to be forced to remain within Yugoslavia, even if they didn't want to, and if they didn't want to, to establish Serbian power and authority and keep Yugoslavia intact that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. Let's see what it says in the transcript here. It says "to establish Serbian authority to keep Yugoslavia intact ..." Did you say we wanted them to remain in Yugoslavia or did you say that we wanted Yugoslavia to remain intact? Did you say that you -- we wanted them to remain in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only wanted but we took political measures via plebiscites and the Assembly of the Serbian people for the Bosniaks and Croats to be influenced, to prevail upon them that they should remain within Yugoslavia, whether it be intact or rump, as it was called at the time, because it was quite obvious that it couldn't actually remain intact, but anyway, for them to remain in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When we lost Yugoslavia and when it was quite clear that we would accept an independent Bosnia and Herzegovina on condition that we were given our constituent unit, did the Serbian Democratic Party have any plans or ideas of in that Serbian Republic -- of not having Muslims and Croats in that Serbian Republic and to persecute them; or did they feel that the minorities should stay, remain, and be protected?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pursuant to the constitution of the 28th of February, 1992, of the Serbian Bosnia and Herzegovina, all citizens had equal rights under the constitution. Now, later on in the war how far the rights of citizens were respected is another matter all together. But constitutionally, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd now like to go back to the subject of Grbavica. Is it correct that until the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic. Mr. Neskovic, before we move on further, can I remind you again to put a pause between the question and the answer for the benefit of the interpreters and us. And I was away yesterday when you gave your evidence in chief due to my personal reasons, but I have yet to read yesterday's transcript but I don't want to miss anything. To the question of Mr. Karadzic in relation to this you said: "The Variant A and B document was not written by well-intentioned officers." And you said: "I believe it was a trick played on the SDS by that group of officers." I was not clear about this. Could you expand on why you said it was a trick. What did you mean by "trick"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We didn't know for a long time who had written the document. Now we know that it was a certain group of officers who formulated the document, and it was a trick because they didn't sign the document. And it is a basic democratic principle that when you write a document, an official document, you sign it so that you can say who you are and who is tabling the document. They didn't want to sign it. That is the first incorrect procedure. The second incorrect procedure was that they forged the header and wrote "Crisis Staff of the SDS" and no such body existed. So what they did was, as a group that was completely outside the SDS, they took it upon themselves, they took the right, to write this document and to put the Crisis Staff of the SDS as the title. And the third incorrect procedure was that they didn't write the document as a proposal, as a draft for further procedure and consideration, but they wrote it as a military system of measures and instructions and acts that were to be implemented in practice, in which security affairs dominated, monitoring, surveillance, mobilisation, replenishment of JNA movements, supplies, the formation of Crisis Staffs, and so on and so forth. It was also incorrect procedure because it wasn't known who they addressed the act -- the document to, who the document was addressed to. In one paragraph they say that the document would be applied only pursuant to a decision of the President Radovan Karadzic, and that the document can be applied only following his decision, if he gave the okay and as he decided. Furthermore, it was a trick because this group saw the interest of retaining Yugoslavia and equated it with the interests of the Serb people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, they equated the Yugoslav interest with the interest of the Serb people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, which was incorrect. The interests of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, their vital interests, were their equality in Bosnia-Herzegovina and not the preservation of Yugoslavia. So this group endeavoured to use the capacities that the SDS had and place them, harness them, to preserve Yugoslavia and to replenish the Yugoslav People's Army as a primary goal to ensure that it was up to strength. So the Yugoslav interest was the primary goal and the Serbian interest was the secondary goal. And it also -- there was also a contradiction there that they wanted to promote to create Serbian authority in municipalities where we were the majority according to A and the minority according to B and to subordinate the members of the other nations to that power and authority, which means the subjugation of the Bosniaks and the Croats to Serb power and creating a policy of fait accompli. And later on, those Bosniaks and Croats would become included, they would be called to become involved and included in that Serb authority and then, together with the Serbs, remain in Yugoslavia and remain supporting the Yugoslav People's Army so that -- perhaps I'm wrong but I personally am of that opinion in reading the document, I see nothing positive in it, nothing positive there, and I see nothing rational either or anything reasonable in its contents. The popular Assembly, the Serbian National Assembly, at the same time passed other acts, documents - and we're talking about December 1991 - to form Serb municipalities, that on Serb territories Serb authority should be set up, that Serb authority in those Serb municipalities where a plebiscite had been held should remain within Yugoslavia; and therefore, this group through this document said nothing new, nothing that hadn't previously been in existence. And now the document was seen to have negative repercussions. And although it wasn't passed by the Serbian Democratic Party and adopted, it was applied nonetheless in practice among the municipalities. That is why I consider this document to be incorrect and a sort of Trojan horse, when you use other people's resources for your own ends and use other people's resources to further your own ends. That's how I understand this. It's like a cuckoo's nest, and the fact that they didn't sign the document was completely incorrect and out of order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Neskovic. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to ask you that when we say "Serb municipality," and you had this in Novo Sarajevo, does that imply that other communities, if they have the conditions to do so in that former municipality, can set up their own municipalities? So when we see "Serb municipality," does that imply that the proposal is that that municipality should be transformed into two or more municipalities?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if the other communities wanted to do so, but the problem was that the other communities did not wish to do so. Then you come into conflict with them, clash with them. And as far as I know, there was only one such municipality, and I think it was in Olovo, where the Bosniak community and the Serbian community agreed to divide the municipality before the war into the Bosniak and the Serbian part and that's how it remained to the end of the war. The problem, as I say, when the other communities did not want to divide up the municipality but wanted to have the whole of the municipality to themselves, then they clashed, and then you had a conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that in more municipalities and not just Olovo where the agreement was adhered to, for example, in Bratunac, in Vlasenica, that there were negotiations in Ilidza and other municipalities, to form administrative power and authority of Serbian local communities peacefully and in the Muslim ones, and that this -- but that this fell through at the beginning of the war, nothing came of it, when the SDA called for it to be rescinded?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that. But I know about Olovo because it was implemented there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have P5 on our screens, that's Variant A and B. Can we have that back on our screens, please, because it might refresh your memory. You might have got things mixed up a bit. My name isn't mentioned there, so may we have P5 on e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for that to come up, did anybody from the centre control you or force you to apply this piece of paper to your municipality, this document to your municipality?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have the next page in Serbian and may we have the English displayed on the split screen as well, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: For justified doubts that forces -- organised forces want to -- activities to be carried out within the framework of the national community of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina for the purpose of implementing the decision --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: May we have a reference as well, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If you look at the first sentence, that because of these doubts about unilateral secession. In point 2 they say that: "The purpose of the tasks, measures, and other activities set forth in these instructions is to enhance mobility and readiness to protect the interests of the Serbian people." And then in point 8, in undertaking all these measures, take care that the respect of national rights is guaranteed and the rights of all nations and their involvement in the organs of power and authority later on set up by the Serbs in the municipalities. Can you see that page relating to defence matters, which is military logic; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Yugoslavia is mentioned here as the vital interest and the preservation of that Yugoslavia, and that everything that should be done should be done to preserve that Yugoslavia. The interests of Yugoslavia and the preservation of Yugoslavia is equated with the interests of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina as being one and the same thing, which it was not.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we now take a look at Variant B.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you said of Variant B that you didn't understand the sense of it because in Variant A we had the power and authority -- or what did you say that you found Variant A nonsensical?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's nonsensical if somebody issues instructions for the Serbs in the municipalities where they are majority should proclaim it to be a Serbian municipality and set up Serbian power and authority, when in the legal municipality Assembly they can -- they had the power and authority to pass decisions and to control the municipality. They didn't need this majority in the Serb municipality. So Variant A seems nonsensical to me. Variant B is more understandable, as far as I'm concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, do you agree that we were the majority and had power and authority in 37 out of the 109 municipalities in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact figures. I don't know how many we had, but roughly 30-odd, yes. I think we had 34 deputies from the municipalities, so that sort of coincides with the number of municipalities. But as I say, I don't know the exact figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, if the Muslims wanted to have their own municipality in that Serbian municipality, that that was an option too?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think the officers here wrote this document and sent it -- addressed it to the Serbs, to harness Serb resources for the preservation of Yugoslavia. They did not have in mind the Bosniaks and Croats here, although they do say that the rights of the Bosniaks and Croats should be protected and later on to include them into Serbian -- into the Serbian authorities, which would already have been set up by then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says here also --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have page 9 of the document displayed, please, 9 of the Serbian and 9 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And we're looking at Variant B. At the access roads to populated areas that: "... secret monitoring and surveillance should be conducted to see the dangers to the Serbian population and to plan corresponding measures for protection as well as envisaging moving and transferring the population and material goods to more secure areas and regions." Now, was this an offensive or defensive measure which is proposed here?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what kind of measure it is but it was illegal as far as the subjects are concerned. If somebody had to sign these measures, then a ministerial council of the Serbian people should have done that, or the Assembly of the Serbian people, and not some group, a group of men who had no position either -- held no position, either in the party or in the authorities. They didn't have the legality to prescribe any measures which the authorities would then have to apply. So you have this group outside the realm of the authorities, prescribing how the authorities should act. Why didn't the authorities do that themselves, propose measures that they were to undertake? So no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. But on the premise that they were hoping that this would be passed at that meeting, is this just a measure for protecting the population, not attacking anyone?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's easy to put things on paper, anything, but in practice it's different. For instance, if you place guards at access ways to a Serb settlement, it is implied you have to give them some weapons, even if it's only hunting rifles. But how can you be sure that the group of guards standing there would act defensively or offensively, if they would commit a crime or not? How are you supposed to control that situation? A key document is missing from Serb policy, a document from the Assembly that was supposed to pass a document about the conduct, responsibilities, and powers of Serb municipalities, and they were supposed to be answerable to the Serb Assembly. This void that was created by the lack of this document was filled, unfortunately, by this paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that they did this in keeping with the Law on All People's Defence and civil protection?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You are not familiar with the law, are you?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know a little bit about it. According to that law, the president of the municipality or the staff of the Territorial Defence and civilian protection under the command of the president of the municipality had the right to propose something like this, because the president of the municipality was by ex officio commander of Territorial Defence. And if anyone could write such a document, it could only have been the president of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that up to this date, 19 December 1991, the SDA already had in every municipality, except Western Herzegovina, a municipal staff of the Patriotic League, they stood guard, they had armed units, the HDZ also had its own armed units and Crisis Staffs, and they introduced Crisis Staffs in municipalities long before us, and Granic, across the border, introduced it in September 1991?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe they had some, but in Novo Sarajevo, as far as I know, there were no Crisis Staffs. I heard of the Patriotic League and Green Berets, but I was not aware of their existence before the 5th of April, when they attacked a police station in Sarajevo. That's really the first time I learned that there was a paramilitary unit called the Green Berets.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your municipality in Novo Sarajevo, on the 5th of April, did the Green Berets attack a police station and kill the policeman Nesa Petrovic [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what was heard from Serb policemen who ran away, they did attack a police station in Hrasno near the mosque. A policeman who was on duty called Petrovic from Mesic, near Rogatica, was killed, and that night the Serb policemen ran away from that police station and came to Vrace, to the cultural hall, and set up a new police station there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Before the front line was established in Grbavica and before our forces came to Grbavica, before the 15th of May, was there a lot of movement from the population -- of the population from one side to another?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe throughout April people went to the other side to work, even later, regardless of the military conflict about the police school at Vrace. War did not spread easily in Sarajevo. People did not accept it. Serbs went to work throughout April. The president of the Executive Board Zarko Djurovic also went to work as long as it was physically possible, and people crossed from one side or another, temporarily or for good, perhaps all the way until June.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Apart from this one day when somebody expelled a certain number of Muslims, was there any organised exchange of population during the war from Grbavica to the city and from the city to Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a republican commission for exchange and its chairman was somebody Bulajic, but I had nothing to do with it. Second, there were exchanges of population run by some people who were on the wrong side of the law in both communities, on both sides. They were not in conflict. So these groups crossed from the Serb to the Bosniak side easily. They had exchanges of population. Some people helped these crossings for money, some exchanged properties. So those affairs were mainly linked to this government commission for exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There's something missing from the transcript: "At their own request." Is it true that people who did not get into official exchanges paid those groups money to help them cross?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about it. I did not witness it, but rumour had it that it was possible to pay someone if you want to cross from one side to another. You pay people who are not exactly on good terms with the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And these regular commissions, they had lists that were made between two exchanges and people applied to be on those lists?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how it went on. They spoke to that government commission. They had nothing to do with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then they crossed by bus across the Brotherhood and Unity Bridge in both directions?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you, I don't know what this commission was doing, how they transported people, how they made lists, what criteria they used, but they were answerable to the government. It was a government affair.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My question was: Is it the case that people applied to be put on those lists and they even looked for connections who could put them on those lists, or were they forced?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All sorts of things went on. Some people wanted to go, some people were forced to go, and some people were forced out of their homes, some were afraid and wanted to go, some wanted to have family reunions. There were all kinds of motives and reasons why people wanted to go from one side or another. Some people were afraid for their lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: A protected witness said once here that his father was put on a list in the federal part of Sarajevo, and when they came to pick him up he refused to go. Is it the case that until the end of the war a certain number of Muslims and Croats stayed in Grbavica, not wanting to leave?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They're in a very difficult situation in the second part of 1992 and it continued to deteriorate throughout the war, but despite that, a significant number of Muslims and Croats stayed in Grbavica throughout the war and they still live there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, today we'll be sitting only till quarter to 2.00. It's time to take a break and we'll break for 20 minutes, after which you will have about half an hour. 20 to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic, yesterday Mr. Tieger, on page 7 of yesterday's transcript, asked you if the members of the Main Board attended sessions of municipal boards to convey the policies on the ground. You said it worked the other way as well, they would also convey demands and requests from the ground. And you said you don't know if the deputies took part in that. Do you know if members of the boards were elected in their constituencies and on that basis were they required to attend meetings and bring the opinions they hear from the ground to the Main Board?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the Statute, 70 per cent of the members of the Main Board had to be elected in electoral units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to ask you, you were in the top echelons of the Serbian Democratic Party. You were part of the Executive Board. Did we ever make or use codes during our conversations, lists of code-names, such as Linden, Eagle, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the communication within the Executive Board and with the Main Board? No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My learned friend Mr. Tieger is very skilful in putting questions, far more skilful than I am, but he asked you a double-barrelled question on page 9 of yesterday's transcript. I'll read it to you now. The second part of the question: [In English] "Although you seem to put a start date on that situation by reference to the time when there was still a joint government, I wanted to ask you how long this was the case, that is, was that the case during the course of the war?" [Interpretation] And the first part of the question you answered "yes." You said: "My authority applied during the war." [In English] "Finally, Mr. Neskovic, you testified that Mr. Karadzic was the undisputed authority in the SDS party and that he, along with Mr. Krajisnik, was the supreme authority of the Serb movement whose policies were implemented through deputies, ministers, MUP officials, through people in government, whether it was joint government or government of the Republika Srpska." [Interpretation] Let me ask you, you know well my position, what I've always stressed is a difference between us and the communists. We don't make decisions, we find solutions. Did I make my own policy according to my wishes and ordered that they be implemented on the ground using deputies or did we together find solutions that were later applied?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Depends on the particular policy. In a specific policy, such as life within the party, such as charting SDS policy and honouring requests from the ground and honouring the opinions of the grass-root level, there was absolute democracy from the grass roots upwards. So as far as life within the party was concerned, there was democracy. But there were some affairs you dealt with outside the party in a parallel track, such as personnel policy, and that I couldn't really call a democratic process. A party won because the entire personnel policy was outside the party. People were chosen by your decision or at the proposal of Dukic and they were answerable to you. So I would give different answers depending on what kind of policies you are talking about. Charting SDS policy and the work of SDS from within was indeed democratic in keeping with the Statute. Now, this parallel activity of yours, where you acted outside the Main Board, outside the Executive Board, without consulting them, was in effect with various other policies, such as the personnel policy and relationships with executive authorities and people in executive power. I couldn't call that democracy because the SDS organs did not take part in that at all. They were in a way deceived.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that in the Deputies Club and in the Assembly I had to fight for my positions and I had to modify them very frequently and accept other people's demands?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you had to fight for your positions within the party, you indeed had to fight for them because you were surrounded by free-thinking people who acted in an environment of democracy. Sometimes the Executive Board would make a decision you didn't like, you would get angry, but you accepted it. So the answer is yes as far as that is concerned. But there are some affairs that you didn't even want to put before the Main Board or the Executive Board, so the Executive Board had no opportunity to discuss it. You did it outside of the SDS with some people whom I don't know in ways that I'm not familiar with and you determined the relationship of the SDS with the government and the personnel policy that was removed from the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were a member of the personnel commission. The president was chairman of the Main Board, Mr. Dukic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree it was our position that in the Ministry of the Interior, for instance, the party should not intervene in personnel issues; instead, the Serbs whom we appointed to these positions should protect the interests of the Serbian people, whereas the party should keep out of it. You object to that; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not exactly so because the party's responsible for the entire governance done by people they elected. The party has great historical responsibility for the activity of people who they never chose or elected or appointed. So the party had the right to appoint people to the MUP, like other sides did, but your position and the position of Dukic was different. You proposed - and it was done -- Serb people were appointed to the MUP who had nothing to do with the Serbian community except Mico Stanisic who ended up as chief of MUP for the city of Sarajevo. Zepinic, Mandic, and others were people whom you and Dukic installed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Through the personnel commission; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was a member of the personnel commission. It was called personnel commission and organisational issues. It never appointed anyone to lower or senior positions. The balance of its activity is zero. Not a single application came before that commission. The commission had no opportunity to have its say, nor was it ever asked about anything. It did absolutely nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We will find transcripts of that commission. Do you remember that Dukic was authorised to negotiate the power-sharing with the SDA party and the Croatian Democratic Union and he was a well-trusted man to whom we entrusted those negotiations?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he was not authorised. He was charged with helping you, and you as president of the party were the real partner for Izetbegovic and Kljujic. Dukic was charged by the party to help you in that. Now, that he transformed his role from assistant to decision-maker about personnel is a different matter.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we briefly look at the War Presidency of Novo Sarajevo, P2568, page 6 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that in Novo Sarajevo you refused to apply the system of the Presidency and you said you didn't need a commissioner either because you were able to hold sessions of the municipal parliament and the municipal government?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did anyone force you to do that or is it the case that these bodies were only envisaged in case the Assembly could not meet?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did exist, but there were three bodies. It was confusing. The commissions, the Presidencies, the Assemblies, that made things confusing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: 25 -- [In English] "And I ask you at the same time whether you became a member of the war commission for the Serbian municipality of Novo Sarajevo ..." [Interpretation] Can we see the next page. [In English] "... in July 1992 and specifically on 21st of July 1992." [Interpretation] Your answer: [In English] "Yes. Although, it is not even clear to me today, not to this day, what this war commission was all about, what was its purpose and what they were supposed to be doing ..." [Interpretation] A bit further down: [In English] "To this day, to be honest, I don't really know what it was all about because at that period, at Grbavica in particular, in the municipality of Novo Sarajevo, the Municipal Assembly and the Executive Committee for the municipality had already been set up ..." [Interpretation] So you refused that because the municipal government was able to operate normally and you didn't need those contingency measures?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was pointless. I told you we set up the Assembly in June, elected members, president of the Executive Board and president of the municipality, and after that it was pointless to establish a commission. Why?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And regarding the previous period you said in your statements and testimony that there was a horrible lack of institutions and it was not able to govern in that complete chaos, there were no people in the government and there was no government in Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I spoke of the government as a closed introverted group that shifted the burden of the war to municipalities and did not look after anything. That's why municipal leaderships were very hard-put, without resources, without assistance, without funding, facing huge problems, and there was little assistance from the government or none at all.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see 1D3487 in e-court, page 40 in Serbian, 37 in English. Page 40 in Serbian and 37 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say here -- we have English -- the English version displayed on the screen. You say the situation was a little tricky and Karadzic says that in the Crisis Staff you had the police and army and the president of the municipality, the Executive Board, the Red Cross, and so on and so forth, as well as the deputies of those municipalities and members of the Main Board of the SDS. I don't think there were any local boards, and that it be a War Presidency and at its head either the president of the SDS or the president of the municipality or Executive Board. And that's where this -- well, we read out this order, Sarovic and I. He played a role there. He advised us not to accept this at all, because that would mean that Sarovic and I would be the heads of the staffs and in command of the army, whereas we weren't capable of commanding the army, let alone taking over the -- a command over the police and army. So he said that we should avoid this at all costs in an elegant way and present arguments supporting that. And you rejected that; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have the next page displayed, both in the Serbian and the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: He says here -- well, the question is: Control through those war commissions was supposed to be established? And you said: Well, you can't exercise control if you have an Assembly, a municipality, that is to say, the three of you have control over an Assembly numbering 30 or 40 people. So that was the reason. Now, do you agree that in many municipalities they did not succeed in establishing a Municipal Assembly and Executive Boards by June and that they needed somebody to come there?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't say. I had limited information during the war in Sarajevo. I didn't actually know what was happening in April/May 1992. I didn't know what was happening outside Novo Sarajevo in the other municipalities, I didn't have any information about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we now have page 46 displayed, please, and it's 43 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The question here is: "From August 1992 onwards until the end of the war what positions did you occupy?" And your answer is: "None. From the 5th of June I did not have a political office. It was a secret vote, democratic. I lost the elections to Branko Radan and he got the majority of votes and became the president of the Executive Board and I did not ..." And then lower down you go on to say that: "... until May 1993 -- I worked on this from June 1992 until May 1993 when I was replaced by the leadership at the time. I don't know why, so I was angry and I left Sarajevo due to my financial crisis and moved," et cetera, et cetera. So that was the denouement of the events in your municipality; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the situation deteriorated. We did have democratic elections. I put myself forward for president of the Executive Board of the local municipality. I lost to the other candidate, who took over the function, and I was given charge of seeing to the refurbishment of the damaged houses and waterworks and the utilities in general. And I did my best to work in the field of the utilities. I went to Belgrade to seek donations for the waterworks, networks, and valves were needed or something like that. And when I returned to Grbavica, I was astonished because they showed me disrespect. They told me that I was replaced from my position. There was another president in 1993, I think it was the man who was killed, Budo Obradovic. They told me, "You've been replaced from your post because you didn't come to work for three days. And based on the law governing labour if you don't come to work for three days you lose your job." And that was ludicrous because they knew where I had gone. So I asked them whether somebody had been appointed to replace me and they said yes, Slavko Tosovic will be doing your job. And I understood at that moment that it was intentional. They replaced me intentionally and under the pretext that the security situation around me was very difficult. And then for economic reasons and to save my life, I took my wife and child and fled to Teslic, and from Teslic I went to Banja Luka, never to return, and that was April 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Obviously it was a well-paid post and so they replaced you?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I think there were lobbies that had already been formed to support each other. People were grouping, forming groups. I wasn't in those lobbies and in their interests linked to business and the accumulation of wealth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we now have page 48 in the Serbian and 45 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said here -- you tell us how many contacts -- how much contact you had with President Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have the Serbian side displayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Anyway, you say that you had around five meetings before 1993, and after 1993 that you had frequent contacts. And your answer when asked why, the purpose of them - next page in the Serbian, please - for what reason you were asked. And then at the bottom of the English page it says: "About five. Throughout the entire war? Well, from 1993 I was in contact with him frequently," you say. And then the question is: "For what reason?" And your answer is: "Well, for example, in 1993 [as interpreted] when the SDS was reactivated in February, I became a member of the Main and the Executive Boards again." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the new party, it wasn't a BH party anymore but a party of all Serb lands, the Main Board was not elected. The same board remained but the Executive Board was replaced, and I became a member of that new Executive Board. The president was Jovo Mijatovic, and I was charged with work in the field, the kind of work that I described earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So at the SDS headquarters they didn't share the attitude towards you that was displayed in the Novo Sarajevo municipality; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, in view of the fact that I don't have enough time, I'd just like to tender this document 1D3487, which is the Defence interview with Mr. Neskovic, and Mr. Neskovic has confirmed his positions, the ones presented during that interview. So I'd like to tender the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't have an objection, Your Honour. On other occasions for other reasons, objections might arise. This document has in fact been referred to extensively, and so various concerns that might otherwise arise I think don't preclude its admission with this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, this will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1278, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we just look at page 50 of this document and then 46 and 47 in English. So 50 in Serbian and 46 and 47 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So while you were in the SDS we had a dynamic relationship. There was a lot of disagreement, contention, but agreement too. But you left the SDS only in 1997; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says here in the interview -- well, your answer was: "No, no, it's not important for me. This is why I left the SDS in 1997, because I didn't agree with what he did in 1996." What did you mean? What is it that happened in 1996 which prompted you and made you feel that the SDS was no longer what it used to be?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at the electoral Assembly in 1996, I understood it that the democratic basis was withering away, so to speak, and I didn't agree with your personnel policy. At the time you wanted to abolish the Executive Board and set up a Presidency which would regionalise the party, and I was opposed to that, and certain personnel, such as Miladin Bosic, you proposed to the SDS Presidency although these were people who had never worked in the SDS. And then through your -- wielding your authority you incorporated Marko Pavic, from Prijedor, into the SDS and he became a member of the Main Board and a deputy although up until then he wasn't even a member of the SDS. Then there was Goran Popovic. And you could see this trend and you could see that you insisted on this, as you did in 1990, that the posts should be occupied through your authority by people who never had anything to do with the SDS previously or very little to do with it, except this time it was at the very peaks of power of the SDS that you wanted to exert your influence to bring in these new people or to elect them or appoint them, appoint people who were in democratic regular SDS functions, procedure -- could never occupy those positions. If you had to go through the municipal boards and the local boards, it would take them a long time to reach the top, but you bypassed that procedure and appointed them to the head of the party so that Mr. Bosic became a member of the Presidency in 1996 and he's the president of the SDS now. And then the other point I disagreed with you on was the relationship towards the international community and the Dayton Accords. We considered that this might not be applied. We didn't see the agreement too seriously, as being too serious, although we did sign it. Now, I might be wrong but I gained the impression that its original democratic source was being lost in the SDS, in the party, its basis and grass roots and so on. And my main objection was certainly the regionalisation of the party with the appointment of the Presidency instead of an Executive Board, and I considered that the party would be regionalised thereby and that the head men would become the sort of ruling princes in their geographic regions and that the party would begin to disintegrate and that it was not good policy and that it was not following on from the organisational set-up of 1991. And I considered that the party would begin to disintegrate through poor organisation and poor personnel policies. So I kept quiet. These were my own musings, and in 1997 I stepped down and left the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you agree that at the time I was already preparing to withdraw because I had promised that after the Assembly, after St. Vitus Day, the end of June, I would leave the party and with Pavic and all those from the left wing, bringing in the left wing, I wanted to strengthen the left wing of the SDS, which all the dissidents of many years held against me. So was that the basis of your criticism, too, for me bringing in part of a leftist-oriented staff?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the basis of my criticism, all power to the people that I mentioned, I have every respect for the people I mentioned, but you did side-step democratic procedure. You can't become a member of the Presidency without going through democratic procedure, party democratic procedures. Now, if the leftists wanted to act democratically, let them form a left-wing party. What did the left-wingers have to do in a Serbian national democratic party? Because it turns out that in SDS you paid more attention to the leftists, left-wingers, than to the SDS parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next page in the English, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, it's now time for you to conclude.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Just one more question, then, and I think we'll find it on page 47 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say: "Yes, I know. In 1996 that there was nothing to do with that, but there are so many events that I haven't explained. I never found out why he did not allow SDS officials to take part in the government they had won. I have never learned why the government banned the SDS and published this in the Official Gazette," and so on and so forth. So that was the prevailing attitude that you had vis-a-vis my need to expand the basis outside the SDS?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. If we're going to extend the party then it's a popular movement, it's not a political party anymore. So I don't think so. My answer is no. Well, if I understood the question correctly, did you ask me whether the prevailing opinion in the SDS was that this is being -- was being held against you? Yes, it was constantly being held against you. You were being criticised for it from 1990 to 1996 by the vast majority of the membership until you withdrew. You persisted in protecting the cadres of the League of Communists, and in 1996 you started bringing them into the top echelon of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Neskovic. I'm sorry that we hadn't had an opportunity to meet before your testimony here in court. Perhaps we would have been able to define questions and answers better, but at any rate thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic, at page 30, I believe, of the statement that you gave to the Karadzic Defence, you indicated that you had looked at some minutes regarding the Crisis Staff in Novo Sarajevo in December of 1991. And the interview indicates that you said that -- something to the effect that I said that the minutes were fabricated, that they were simply untrue. Now, I don't know if that's a translation problem, but I wanted to look at those minutes and quickly look at what you said about those minutes in the course of your testimony in the Krajisnik case. Those minutes are P2575. Now, those minutes are dated the 23rd of December, 1991, just a few days after the distribution of the Variant A and B document by Dr. Karadzic. The document refers to "the materials received from the SDS BH Main Board." Immediately after that, as we can see, it refers to the first degree or step, "prvi stepen" in the B/C/S. It lists 11 items which, as you confirmed in your Krajisnik testimony, are precisely the number of items listed in the Variant A and B document. And the entries in P2575 correspond to the entries in the Variant A and B document. For example, item 2 of the Variant A and B document in the first level Variant A refers to a municipal secretariat. We see here in this document item 2 refers to that. Item 3 similarly refers to a Crisis Staff, and so on, in terms of the persons who were assigned to various tasks as well. Now, is it correct, Mr. Neskovic, that when you reviewed these documents during the course of your Krajisnik case, you didn't say that the minutes were fabricated. You simply expressed the observation that, according to you, something was missing from that document and also a follow-up document that you saw, and that was that you couldn't see who the commander of the Crisis Staff was. And I refer you and the other participants to the transcript pages 16671 through 72. In short, Mr. Neskovic, that was the issue or concern that you raised during the course of your Krajisnik testimony? Yes, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
