utterances.text: I apologise if a statement of mine has been misunderstood. It's my duty to explain. This document is not a forgery. It is a document of the Crisis Staff of Novo Sarajevo. Based on the contents, it is Variant A. So Variant A is being applied here. My criticism and the remark I made was that there was no signature as to who the command of the Crisis Staff was, although, according to Variants A and B, it should have been the president of the Executive Board of the Zarko Djurovic -- of the municipality Zarko Djurovic. But I have to add that Zarko Djurovic as president of the Executive Board and Milivoje Prijic as president of the Municipal Board of the Serbian Democratic Party, although they were -- they mutually clashed, both of them had great reservations towards the application of Variant A and B. And quite obviously here there was a meeting, a certain meeting took place, the meeting was called the Crisis Staff and everything is exact, everything written here is exact. So it's not a forgery, it's not falsified. But if you look at it, we are lacking points 4 and 5. So all the other points are listed, except for points 4 and 5, which were the key points in Variant A. Point 4 related to the formation of the Crisis Staff and point 5 also relates to something about whether mobilisation or -- regarding the JNA or the establishment of power -- bodies of power and authority. So perhaps points 4 and 5 were the most important ones which are missing here. So all the other points are being addressed here, but there's no readiness here to set up a separate Novo Sarajevo municipality and its separate bodies set up. So it a document which is valid, is accurate, but my objection was and remark in Krajisnik was a dilemma I had. I don't know whether Djurovic attended the meeting at all, and I see that he's not signed here, whereas he should have been the president. So that was my dilemma, who the head of the Crisis Staff was, otherwise I have no criticisms to make or objections to make to the document itself. It is an original document, a valid document, and that is the Novo Sarajevo document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic, just to -- before we leave this document, we'll do so quickly. Just to clarify the identification of the commander and his deputy commander. You've already indicated that according to the Variant A and B document, the commander would be the president of the Executive Committee or president of the Municipal Assembly. Therefore, please look at item 3 where it indicates "Formiran Krizni Stab," et cetera, and then it says "odredjen komandant po funkcija," "by function"; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, then by function it's Zarko Djurovic, president of the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. If I could turn next quickly to a point that was raised at some length during the course of your cross-examination and that was with respect to regionalisation. It appeared that during the course of your discussions with Mr. Karadzic yesterday and in the course of your interview with the Defence, you focused to some extent on Banja Luka and appeared to lay responsibility for regionalisation on the Banja Luka authorities, and that was beginning at page 8 of your interview, and asserted that the regions were formed because of the war in Croatia with other regions following Krajina at least on paper, and that was at page 14 of your interview and I believe at transcript pages 14255 through 56. Now, first of all, before the war in Croatia, Mr. Neskovic, it's correct that communities of municipalities were formed; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And are you aware of the extent to which the accused spoke about or indeed spoke about the communities of municipalities, followed by the autonomous regions, and other steps as having been formulated in advance, leading to the establishment of the organs and entity of Republika Srpska; do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew about three different processes of regionalisation, some intertwined, some running parallel. If I might explain, one process is the deputy -- the deputies, the Serb deputies, did. They started with this process from the 24th of October and ended by forming the Republika Srpska. The second process was done by the municipalities from Banja Luka, Herzegovina, Romanija, forming communities of municipalities in the spring of 1991. And in September 1991 they transformed it to become the Serbian autonomous regions, so that's the second line or course of regionalisation. And the third branch was the work that Izetbegovic and Karadzic did on the topic of regionalisation. So these three lines, sometimes they ran parallel, sometimes there was an intersection. After the 24th of October, 1991, the lines merged in a way to become one line, one course, which resulted in the formation of the entity the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you aware of the plenary or symposium or consultation, whatever its particular designation, of municipal, regional, and republic-level SDS organs on September 7th, 1991, regarding regionalisation?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I attended several of those meetings. There was perhaps one meeting dealing with that issue in the MIG building near Pale. I don't know if that's the meeting you mean. That meeting discussed the issue of realisation. It was a catering facility. It was not a very specific systematic discussion with specific conclusions. Now, whether there were other meetings apart from that, I can't recall now. But there was that one meeting in the MIG building about regionalisation I know about because I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let's take a look at 65 ter 16722. That's the minutes of the third meeting of the Executive Board of the Serbian Democratic Party held on 16th September 1991. First item on the agenda is the decision on the appointment of the regionalisation staff, which was considered and adopted in accordance with the conclusion adopted at the consultations in Pale. And then further on down the page it continues with: "... the agreement to hold the joint meeting with members of the Executive Board, the regional staff, our members in government to formulate issues and establish tasks in accordance with the importance and urgency of these issues." So that meeting was focused on the conclusions adopted at the earlier meeting to which I referred and took action in accordance with it; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if it relates to that meeting, but as far as regionalisation is concerned, it was part of the official activity of the board and the party believed that regionalisation is a legitimate policy aimed against centralisation. So the party was involved in decentralisation. Whether this is a reference to that particular meeting or consultation, I can't know. You know, this consultation may not have -- may not have resulted in any specific conclusions and then at this meeting -- those in the board heard about this meeting in the MIG building at Pale and they wanted to discuss regionalisation in a more substantial way. It's possible that from this point on the party was more focused on regionalisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender that document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2524, Your Honours -- 2584.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And can we also call-up, please, next 65 ter 17542 -- no, I'm sorry, the next one would be -- my apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I believe that would be 06602.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic, this is the fifth meeting of the Executive Committee held on 7 November 1991. The fifth item on the agenda is "Report on Regionalisation."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if we could turn to item 5 at page 5 of the English. And if the Registrar could find for the witness item 5 in the B/C/S, which will be toward the end of the document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It indicates, among other things, that: "... conditions should be created in the region which would allow the observance that the principle that every region should include and incorporate the national and territorial treasures. The aim is to create a Serbian Bosnia and Herzegovina within Yugoslavia and to establish relations with the Muslims and the Croats based on the confederate principle." So, Mr. Neskovic, the Executive Board continued to work on regionalisation, and in particular identifying the portions of territory within Bosnia and Herzegovina which would incorporate within Serbian Bosnia and Herzegovina the national and territorial treasures sought by Serbs?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender this document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P2585, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And finally if we could turn to 01472.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: These reflect minutes of the main and executive -- the Main Board and Executive Committee or -- held on December 3rd, 1991. Again, we see regionalisation on the agenda on the first page, and I wanted to ask you this. You had earlier said, or just a moment ago, Mr. Neskovic, that regionalisation was about breaking centralisation or against centralisation. If I could turn you to the first entry reflecting the comments of Mr. Karadzic at that meeting, and that's on page 2 of the English and I believe the same page of the B/C/S. Dr. Karadzic states: "They want a sovereign Bosnia - they adopted in the Assembly and seek international co-operation - in that case, by holding on to our territories, we will prevent their sovereignty." Mr. Neskovic, when you spoke about regionalisation being an approach to resist centralisation, that was a reflection of -- was that a reflection of regionalisation's impact on preventing the sovereignty or the attempted sovereignty and independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the efforts by Bosnian Muslim and Croat authorities to assert sovereignty?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The regionalisation in which the SDS took active part implied two consequences. One was an aspiration to prevent the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina through regionalisation and keep the entire Bosnia within Yugoslavia; or, if that was impossible, to keep one part of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Yugoslavia, the area where the Serbs had had a plebiscite and where they had a majority. That was one of the consequence, keeping Yugoslavia as a priority objective. And this consequence dominated all the way up to end 1991 and the conclusions of the Badinter Commission. After that, when the Yugoslav option fell through and when the Serbian regionalisation as a way to preserve Yugoslavia fell through, then regionalisation acquired another objective, accepting an independent Bosnia but transformed from within, on a regional basis. So the regionalisation had both consequences, one of them prevalent in one period and the other prevalent in another period. So you are right, up to the end of 1991 the first consequence of regionalisation was preserving Yugoslavia and preventing Bosnia from becoming independent.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender this document, if I haven't done so already, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask for a clarification. In Serbian we see something said by Professor Milojevic. I want to avoid confusion. What is written here is said by Professor Milojevic, not Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are we looking at the same page? Mr. Tieger, can you help us on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: There is a reference to Mr. Milojevic by Dr. Karadzic, but the speaker is Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Maybe he could tell us where in the Serbian the name "Karadzic" appears. I don't see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's why I asked that question, whether we are on the same page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could -- well, I'm not going to have -- be able to read that as quickly as I would like under the circumstances. We can address that issue, but I think the witness's answer referred more to the concept of the regionalisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, the Serb version is of seven pages so that we can look at it later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't you proceed. We'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P2586, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic, yesterday there was reference to -- well, yesterday and throughout the course of your testimony and indeed in the interview, reference to Main Boards and Executive Boards, implementing policies through those organs on one hand and through deputies, the Deputies Club and the Assembly on the other. First of all, with respect to the deputies and their implementation of policy, either party policy or the policy of the leaders of the Serb movement, it's correct, isn't it, that the deputies must -- were required to promote party policy because of the SDS because it was the party that elected them. And I refer you in particular to page 14238 of your testimony in Krajisnik. That's correct, isn't it, Mr. Neskovic, that you stated that the deputies should promote party policy because it was the party that elected them?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. The deputies in their own parties promote and implement party policy, and the deputies of the SDS, as far as I know, implemented, realised, and promoted the programme of the Serbian Democratic Party and its policies, but they were not policed by the Executive Board or the Main Board. They were independent in implementing party policy.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in fact, was it the case that deputies could be dismissed and their mandates withdrawn for abandoning the political stances of the party or the party programme? For example, this Court has received evidence - and that's contained in the 51st Assembly Session held on the 14th and 15th of June, 1995 - that the mandates of Andjelko Grahovac, Risto Jugovic, Milan Trbojevic and Milan Tesic were withdrawn for their abandonment of the programme and the adopted political stances of the party?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about those two cases, but the party did not legally have the right to withdraw a mandate. The party was able, as far as I know, to replace -- to throw out Grahovac and Trbojevic from the party, but in this case I'm not sure. The party did not have a mandate to replace deputies. There was no mechanism for something like that. I don't know the details about Grahovac and Trbojevic. The thing was Trbojevic was that he had changed his electoral base, so something -- with Grahovac it was something else. I'm sorry I'm not able to assist you more, but I'm not sure if the party threw out these deputies. I don't think it was entitled to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, despite the legality of such an action, do you know that that decision was based on -- or that withdrawal of the mandate was based on a decision signed by Dr. Karadzic, that's 65 ter 18028, no need to call it up now, which in turn was based on conclusions of the Main Board reflected in 65 ter 18026? But did you know about that progression, Mr. Neskovic, decisions by the party officials and the ultimate withdrawal of the mandate of those deputies?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the details. I was probably there at that meeting too, and I think it was done for the first time in the party in 1995. If this was really done, I think the party was wrong, but I don't know the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Then I'll submit those by way of bar table to expedite the process, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic, one further point, I think you mentioned at page -- I think it was -- well, I'd have to find the page, but you mention in your interview with the Defence that there were approximately seven to eight deputies who were members of the Main Board. So those persons were in a position, each one of them, to advise the Main Board of developments within the Deputies Club and the Assembly; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Objection, leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, were those persons, Mr. Neskovic, in a position based on their positions as deputies and members of the Deputies Club to advise the Main Board of developments and policy arising in the Deputies Club?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were eight or ten of them. They were indeed in a position to inform the Main Board about the work of the Deputies Club. They were in a position to advise and recommend, but the feedback mechanism, that is, the influence of the Main Board on the Deputies Club did not work, that they were indeed, yes, in a position to inform and advise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in fact, I count approximately 14 deputies who were also SDS Main Board members during 1991/1992. Let me mention the names and ask you to confirm that -- whether or not these persons were Main Board members. Milovan Bjelosevic, Mr. Buha or Dr. Buha, Dusko Kozic, Momcilo Krajisnik, Vojo Kupresanin, Grujo Lalovic, Dr. Milutin Najdanovic, Miladin Nedic, Milan Novakovic, Srdjo Srdic, Veljko Stupar, Dobrivoje Vidic, Milenko Vojinovic, and Goran Zekic.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were members of the Main Board, as far as I remember, and I knew all of these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Neskovic, just a couple more points. In your interview with the Defence you described the -- and I think in your testimony yesterday as well you asserted that there was an absence of telephone contact in Novo Sarajevo between April 10th and May 10th, 1992. Now, first of all, during that period of time were you able to have contact with police officials or military officials in the Novo Sarajevo area?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With police officials we could have contact without any problem. We just had to travel all day to Sarajevo to see them. But with military officials, I believe we had only one contact at a joint meeting in Vogosca, where General Galic made an address. We were listening to a speech he gave. And with police officials we could easily have contact except we had to travel one whole day around the city to get to Ilijas, Hadzici, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And with respect to telephone contact, Vrace was in Novo Sarajevo; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Vrace was in Novo Sarajevo. It's a hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And do you know the extent to which officials in Vrace were able to communicate with telephone -- by telephone during that period of time with Bosnian Serb officials in Pale and elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. Perhaps the only possibility would be to call the police school at Vrace and through them get into contact with the Serbian leadership at Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Finally, Mr. Neskovic, there were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, I'm not sure if the LiveNote is working at this moment. I don't think that -- yes. How much more do you have for your re-direct, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Certainly no more than five minutes, Your Honour, if that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Finally, Mr. Neskovic, particularly during the latter part of your cross-examination you discussed the Variant A and B document in -- and offered some views about military officials who were -- were or may have been involved in its drafting. Are you asserting that you know who wrote this -- who drafted this document, Mr. Neskovic, or were you simply offering views based on the question that -- and proposition that the accused put to you, that is, that it was drafted by retired JNA officials? And I ask that in particular because, among other things, in your interview you said at page 60 -- well, let me just ask you that question first because I understood you to say in your testimony in Krajisnik --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NESKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know who wrote the document A and B, and the information that it was written by a group of retired officers was something that I learned later, following a trial in this courtroom. I believe it was Mr. Karadzic who said during an examination that it was written by a group of frightened military retirees. And based on that and accepting it as true, although I only heard it following the trial on the internet, am I saying that it was written by them. At the time, I had no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Neskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That concludes my re-direct examination, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, might I just ask one question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, and I would also note that the reference in the December 3rd document to Mr. Karadzic can be found at the top of page 3 in the B/C/S as I understand it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. About what, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to ask the witness whether he knows for sure that it wasn't the SDS organs who wrote the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do know that. The SDS organs, the legal commission, and the Executive Board did not write this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The witness has already answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That concludes your evidence, Mr. Neskovic. On behalf of the Bench and the Tribunal as a whole, I appreciate your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But we will rise all together. We will have a break for half an hour and resume at 12.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Treanor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Treanor, you weren't in court when the case had to be adjourned. I'm sorry that you weren't there to listen to it. You were out of court for a good reason, and I hope you don't think that your personal circumstances were not taken into account as much as they could be in the circumstances in which we faced ourselves. So I just wanted to make that plain, that it was a pity you weren't in court, but in the circumstances it wasn't possible.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I understand completely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now it's for you, Mr. Karadzic, to continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Dr. Treanor.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: From Friday to today, did you have any contacts with the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did anybody explain to you why we had the adjournment or postponement of your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you whether you knew that the Prosecution had had talks with Mr. Jovan Cizmovic and that the material did exist in the OTP?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which material?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The interview that the Prosecutor had with Mr. Jovan Cizmovic. I think there were two interviews in actual fact.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with those interviews.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you think that there's other material which has not been placed at your disposal -- that had not been placed at your disposal before you concluded your report?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How can he know that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you. You're quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll deal with that tomorrow, but now I'd like to continue where we left off, Dr. Treanor, and we left off discussing the 19th of December. Do you agree with me that the Muslim-Croat portion of the government and the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, ignoring the opposition of the Serb members of these organs, asked for international recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as you state in paragraph 95 of your report, 1225?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that this initiative, this call for independence, could only have come from the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina and not from the government or Presidency?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that it is constitutional matter and the change in the nature of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, would you agree that it is, in fact, constitutional matter?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that generally that's true, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that Badinter responded to that request and that opinion number 4 relates to the request?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have 65 ter 5816 on e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that Mr. Badinter responded to the initiative from Bosnia-Herzegovina? Have you had a chance to look at this opinion, opinion number 4?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's take a look at the first page. There's some general details there, and in point 4 it says: "Letter of the 27th of December, 1991, from the President of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina to Lord Carrington ..." So in that letter -- [In English] I'll read it in English. "Letter of 27th of December, 1991, from the President of the Presidency of the SRBH to Lord Carrington, Chairman of the Conference on Yugoslavia, on the formation of an 'Assembly of the Serbian People in Bosnia-Herzegovina ...'" [Interpretation] And then it says further on --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, may we have the next page displayed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English] "The current Constitution of the SRBH guarantees equal rights for 'the nations of Bosnia-Herzegovina - Muslims, Serbs and Croats - and the members of the other nations and ethnic groups living in its territory.'" [Interpretation] And then it would be advisable to look at the whole of the next page, but I don't want to read it out. Let's look at point 3, the commission notes. [In English] "A. That the declarations and the undertakings above were given by the Presidency and the Government of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but that the Serbian members of the Presidency did not associate themselves with those declarations and undertakings ..." [Interpretation] And paragraph 3: "... outside the international framework of the SRBH, on 10th of November, 1992, the 'Serbian people of Bosnia-Herzegovina' voted in a plebiscite for a common Yugoslav state. On 21st of December, 1992, an 'Assembly of the Serbian People of Bosnia-Herzegovina' passed a resolution calling for the formation of a 'Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina' in a federal state of Yugoslavia if the Muslim and Croat communities of Bosnia-Herzegovina decided to 'change their attitude towards Yugoslavia'" --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, I'm sure Dr. Karadzic just misspoke but that was a reference to 21 December 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then I made a slip of the tongue. Probably I read it out wrongly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Anyway, point 4 -- or rather, it's a continuation. [In English] "On the 9th of January, 1992, this Assembly proclaimed the independence of the 'Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.'" [Interpretation] Paragraph 4: [In English] "In these circumstances, the Arbitration Commission is of the opinion that the will of the peoples of Bosnia-Herzegovina to constitute the SRBH as a sovereign and independent State cannot be held to have been fully established. "This assessment could be reviewed if appropriate guarantees were provided by the Republic applying for recognition, possibly by means of a referendum of all the citizens of the SRBH without distinction, carried out under international supervision." [Interpretation] Do you agree that the Assembly of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina reacted to this request from the Muslim-Croat part of the government and Presidency, it reacted with a call for them to rescind the decision or the Serbian Assembly would proclaim the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that the response of the Arbitration Commission to this same matter was this opinion listed under opinion number 4?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in general terms, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I tender this into evidence, please, opinion number 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This is part of Badinter opinion. We're admitting only three pages from the document. Very well. That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1279, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's have a look at D86 now, page 96 of the Serbian and 46 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At the Assembly of the Serbian people, the -- an opposition deputy, Dr. Kalinic, on the occasion spoke and said -- or rather, did you notice his speech, the speech he delivered in the Assembly of the Serb people? Paragraph 4, page 96 in Serbian and 46 in English.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, which session is this?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The 21st of December, the Assembly of the Serb people after what the government did, coming after what the government did?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I read that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'd like to draw your attention to the reply made by Mr. Kalinic, who at the time was in the Serbian Assembly but not a member of the SDS, but a member of the reformists. It says: "Please, I can state in my own personal name - and I hope that this is your opinion too - that nobody has the right to prevent the Muslim people, which are people with their own tradition and history and sovereign rights, to found their own sovereign national state, but on territories, to use the term used by Mr. Izetbegovic, which they make viable and prosperous in the long run. Similarly, the Serbian people, and I presume the Croatian people as well, would not even dream of having their nation states, that is, establishing independent political institutions on the territories that they cannot make viable and prosperous in the long run." Do you remember that Mr. Izetbegovic before the election said if Croatia steps down from Yugoslavia then Bosnia will too. If we can't have the whole of Bosnia, then the territories will step down which the Muslims can make viable and prosperous?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with that particular remark of Dr. -- Mr. Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the intercepts and other material, did you come across confirmation that the initial idea on the division of Bosnia, or rather, the transformation of Bosnia came from Alija Izetbegovic and that I was surprised and informed President Milosevic about that, whereas Mr. Zulfikarpasic wrote about it in his book?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as to the idea coming from Mr. Izetbegovic, I'm -- I can't recall seeing anything that specific. I'm aware of -- of course of some of these other conversations in which the idea is discussed with Mr. Milosevic, and again the -- referring back to the 30 September 1991 Deputies Club meeting at which Dr. Karadzic pointed out that Mr. Izetbegovic was willing to discuss the subject of regionalisation. But to say that he was the originator of the idea, I can't recall anything that specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you know that the Zagreb morning paper first publicised the idea on the cantonisation of Bosnia and that Mrs. Plavsic stated her views on that and said that the idea was interesting as food for thought?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall that. I'm not -- I don't think I'm familiar with that. I'm not sure what date you're referring to, but I can't recall anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, we'll have the documents by tomorrow. But let me ask you this: Did you note Dr. Kalinic's speech at the Assembly held on the 21st of December, the one in which he invokes the right of all three peoples to have sovereign control of their life in the territories where they are in the majority and that he recognises that right for both the Muslim and Croatian people?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, as I said, I have read that speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you consider that it would be useful had the view of Dr. Kalinic been included in your report, for instance?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't -- not particularly. I don't see any great difference between that and what the SDS itself was suggesting at that time, that is, that the peoples who wanted to leave Yugoslavia were free to leave, but the Serbs would stay. In regard to Dr. Kalinic, I would have to point out that in my recollection at this time he was an independent deputy in the Assembly of the SRBiH. I believe he had left the reformist party. And I would also point out that he was a member of the Assembly of the Serbian people at this time, as you pointed out, an Assembly that originated in a meeting of the SDS Deputies Club. In effect, he had joined that Deputies Club - if I can put it that way. And of course later on, later years, Dr. Kalinic did join the SDS and was, in fact, the president of the SDS. So I don't see any great distinction between his views and those of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to draw your attention to paragraph 103 of your report, 1225, where you say that Professor Koljevic had a meeting with the Croatian leadership in order to discuss the ethnic division of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Can you find that passage? [In English] "Thus, in January 1992, while the BSL was still exploring the possibility of a negotiated solution with the Croatian leadership, Karadzic's political ally, Koljevic, urged the reorganisation of Bosnia within the aim of the homogeneity of certain areas." [Interpretation] Do you see that paragraph? And you refer to the transcript of the talk with President Tudjman, that President Koljevic and President Boras had, or rather, the members of the BH Presidency?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is paragraph 103?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I see that paragraph -- I don't see all the words that you've read, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English] "Thus, in January 1992 ..." [Interpretation] You have that in hard copy.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have P986 displayed, please, that's the transcript of the talk with President Tudjman, P986, page 46 of the Serbian and 35 of the English. Fine. May we get the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's see what Franjo Boras, member of the Presidency of BH, has to say on behalf of the Croats. "I would add to your question, Mr. President, that the Muslims would not gladly accept this and that they would not be glad to hear of these discussions of ours this evening. Their concept with Alija as the head, a sovereign Bosnia and Herzegovina as a civic state, and by that very fact, as Professor Koljevic has already pointed out, they would like to ensure the pre-eminence of the Muslim people in Bosnia and Herzegovina and the gradual eradication of the two peoples, especially the Croatian people ..." Did you take into account these fears that Mr. Boras expressed?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I -- I've read the transcript and I've given my summary of that meeting in this paragraph. So to that extent, I took them into account, yes. The -- by the way, Franjo Tudjman had similar fears about the demographic threat presented by the Muslims because of their birthright to those that we've seen emanating from SDS circles.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have page 47 next, please, to hear what Professor Koljevic had to say. It's page 37 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Professor Koljevic, let's see what he has to say. "Let me tell you what the German ambassador said to me in a long talk. A sentence emerged because paradoxically they think that we would be much better firemen, Croats and Serbs, for isolating the Muslims in Bosnia and Herzegovina who then would not have the possibility of linking up further to those transversals. "And now you see what role is being ascribed to our people -- what role is being ascribed to our peoples ..." Do you remember that there was the firm conviction that many European countries considered that the Serbs and Croats had to be kept in Bosnia, so as to control the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm aware that that view was attributed to unnamed European states or statesmen by the Bosnian Serb leaders.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Look, please, what President Tudjman says. "Yes, but it's not the opinion only of the Eff, but the whole world is afraid of what you have called the green transversal and it's the creation of an Islamic state in Europe." Did you take into account the opinion expressed by President Tudjman, that it's not only Minister Eff's opinion but that the linking-up of Bosnia with the Islamic world through this green transversal is a great threat to Europe?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, I've read this transcript and I gave my summary of what I believed to be the relevant points of the meeting. If I could just comment that the idea of the green transversal is -- or relates to a -- some sort of, if I could put it, Muslim corridor or bridge from Bosnia to -- through the Balkans to Turkey. One link in that chain would have been the area in Serbia called the Sandzak, which is -- which borders on Bosnia and has a large Muslim minority. So this was an idea again ascribed to various people that -- but in any case was seen as a threat to Serbia itself. Part of the reason for the strategic goal relating to the Drina Valley that we discussed during my testimony was to prevent the creation of such a transversal by interposing Serbian territory in the Drina Valley between the Muslims in -- between the Muslims west of the Drina and those in Sandzak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll come back to that strategic objective number 3. But your paragraph 103 does not reflect what President Tudjman says. Tudjman is not worried about Serbia at all; he's worried about Europe. And he claims that it's a threat to Europe, not Serbia; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that seems to be what he's saying, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see page 54 of Serbian and 42 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here Professor Koljevic speaks about the need to restructure municipalities. Mr. Lerotic, advisor to Tudjman, asks: Is it possible? Koljevic says it's possible to separate part of the municipalities where they have a hinterland. And let's see what Boras says. He's a deputy to the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina. "According to the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina, there is an option, a possibility, for a Municipal Assembly to take a decision to hold the referendum in a local community where there is only one ethnic group and the people voted a referendum to create a separate local community, on joining another municipality, et cetera, and then the Assembly just has to confirm it. "That is an option that existed in the current constitution ..." Do you know about this? Do you know that what Mr. Boras is saying here is correct, it is a possibility envisaged by the constitution?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall that specific provision. I wouldn't doubt that it's in there, but I can't recall it offhand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We've seen that this meeting between Professor Koljevic and the Croatian leadership, Serbs and Croats are convinced that the European community is insisting on a unified Bosnia-Herzegovina because the Islamic factor needs to be controlled. Do you agree that due to the fact that world politics are beyond the rights of Bosnia and Herzegovina, we accepted that Bosnia and Herzegovina be independent on the condition that it be restructured before independence? In other words, do you agree that Serbs had abandoned their constituent status and stopped insisting on Yugoslavia, on the condition that Bosnia be transformed and that Serbs get something out of it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's sort of a complicated issue. I think we've discussed before in my testimony that -- and in the reports that at this time the SDS leadership was insisting on precisely that point, that if BH was going to be independent it would have to be transformed first and then they would accept independence via a referendum after an agreement was reached. And negotiations were taken up under international auspices in February to that effect. As for giving up on Yugoslavia, that's where it gets complicated. In fact, the declaration of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina refers to it as being part of Yugoslavia, which Bosnia was at that time. And the constitution of the Bosnian Serb republic adopted on the 28th of February, 1992, also states that the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina is part of Yugoslavia and that provision of the constitution was never changed in the -- during the following years, the years of conflict. There was some discussion of doing so in the late summer of 1992 in the Bosnian Serb Assembly, but the idea of eliminating that clause of the constitution was rejected. One of the reasons for doing that is because the plebiscite of the Serbian people, which had taken place in November 1991, had come out for exactly that, for remaining in Yugoslavia. And the plebiscite was for the Bosnian Serbs a -- a very strong argument in favour of the legitimacy of their desire to remain in Yugoslavia. We've seen reference to that in the Badinter Commission opinion, which referred to that plebiscite. So, on the one hand, they were willing to -- what -- "they" being the SDS leadership were willing to accept a transformed independent Bosnia, but only basically as an interim stage before the Serbian portion of that Bosnia which they wanted to be a confederation, which in Serbian parlance means not a state, a confederation is not a state, that the Serbian portion would at some later date join together with other Serbian entities to form a single Serbian state.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Doctor, do you make a distinction between the outcome of political negotiations and an outcome that comes after the outbreak of the war? In other words, do you know that in case of a political outcome we undertook not to have any territories annexed to anything, and that didn't happen because Bosnia and Herzegovina was plunged into war?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the negotiations that I'm referring to, generally referred to as the Cutileiro negotiations, never came to an agreement. There were various documents which were to serve as bases for further negotiations. And the point that you mentioned is referred to in those bases, but there never was an agreement to that effect. And I think that the whole thrust of Bosnian Serb policy in this area would have ultimately led to -- or that they would have wanted ultimately to join a -- together with other Serbs in a single state, whatever that particular agreement may have said - and it didn't say anything because it wasn't an agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I strenuously deny that, Doctor, and I would like to call paragraph 96 of your report. And I put to you the position of the Defence. In the event of an agreed solution, an agreed arrangement, the Serbs had undertook to stay within Bosnia as long as the borders of Bosnia are respected, whereas in the event of war, any outcome becomes possible. Is that correct? If it's easier for you to wait for the paragraph, 96, to be on the screen, you say: [In English] "Karadzic also informed the Assembly rather cautiously of a new approach to the future of BH on the 21st of December, speaking for the first time about transformation of Bosnia in discussing ongoing negotiations with the Muslims and Croats leaders in B&H. "Karadzic noted, 'I can inform you that our first proposal and this is according to the mandate you have given us, that is, the option preferred by the Serbian people was the preservation of a united, equal Bosnia and Herzegovina as a federal unit within Yugoslavia ...' However, 'we put forward another proposal which incorporates the idea of a fundamental transformation of Bosnia and Herzegovina into a union of the three equal national communities ...' "More specifically, 'What we have offered is a solution according to which Bosnia and Herzegovina would become a confederation based on territorial and individual autonomy, i.e., mutual independence ...' Further, the Bosnian Serb leaders had suggested ..." and you are quoting, "'... the establishment of three entities in BH, which would not threaten or confront each other ... so that common institutions could be formed at the level of BH, that is, the existing Republic of BH.'" [Interpretation] Finished quote. [In English] "Finally, both the Serbian and Croatian BH might be able to form links with Yugoslavia and Croatia respectively." [Interpretation] Doctor, do you know that every day there was some conference going on, the Cutileiro or the Lisbon conference, then the Vance-Owen conference, then Stoltenberg, then the Contact Group, and then it all ended with the Dayton Accords and it was ended precisely in this way, not three but two units with special parallel connections with Croatia on the one hand and Yugoslavia, that is to say Serbia, on the other?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know there were many conferences and negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That's not an answer that can satisfy me. Can you point out where exactly we said that the agreed arrangement of Bosnia and Herzegovina would be violated by our secession? In other words, do you agree that in the event of war our undertakings to preserve Bosnia in its borders do not apply any longer?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let's take the situation before the war. I think you wanted to draw a distinction. The speech that I've referenced in this paragraph is, in my view, an attempt to alert the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, including members of the SDS, that it wasn't going to be as simple as everyone, that is, the Bosnian Serbs, had thought, as simple as just remaining in Yugoslavia, as per the results of the plebiscite. I think I discussed this in -- during my direct examination. The leaders in Belgrade certainly would not be able to permit that for international reasons, and they were -- had to go ahead and form a new Yugoslavia consisting of only two republics, and that including the Serbian territories in Bosnia and Croatia. So there was going to have to be some sort of intermediate stage and this is the beginning of the public mention of such an alternative which eventually caused some dissatisfaction among various Bosnian Serb circles, which I didn't go into. However, I would note the use of the word "confederation" here. I mentioned that earlier. Serbian leaders in Belgrade and in Bosnia were very insistent that a confederation was not a state, and therefore they had rejected the idea of turning the SFRY into a confederation instead of being a federation. Because if it were a confederation, then the Serbs would not all be in one state. So the position that the SDS did indeed adopt at the beginning of the Cutileiro negotiations called for the creation of a confederation in Bosnia, that is, a confederation of Bosnia which in their conception would not have been a state but which would have consisted of three different entities, and there were repeated references by Dr. Karadzic and other leaders to the fact that the Serbian entity and indeed the Croatian entity would be free to enter into any type of relations that they deemed fit in the future with either Serbia or Croatia. That's all before the war started. They didn't say that during the negotiations per se, but they were saying that among themselves, that we will be free to associate with Serbia in the future in any manner that we desire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see P782, page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It is the Defence case, Dr. Treanor, that if Bosnia and Herzegovina was to be outside of Yugoslavia, it should have been like Switzerland. Do you remember our proposal that Bosnia-Herzegovina be turned into a Switzerland on the Balkans? Wherever there are 20.000-plus people in one area of the same ethnicity, ethnic cantons can be formed. Yes or no, do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I vaguely remember something like that, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see page 2. I don't know which page it is in Serbian. I think it's the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English] "Bosnia and Herzegovina would continue to have its existing borders and neither the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina nor the governments of the constituent units will encourage or support claims to any part of its territory by neighbouring states." Number 3: "Sovereignty resides in the citizens of the Muslim, Serb and Croat nations and other nations and nationalities who would realise it through their civic participation in the constituent units and the central organs of the republic." [Interpretation] That's on page 1 --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which document is this, I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Page 1, items 2 and 3. [In English] "Independence." [Interpretation] The heading is "Independence." And further on, on page 3. Do you agree that this was a paper on the basis of which it had been agreed that the future Bosnia-Herzegovina would look this way? It's better known as the Cutileiro Plan.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Page 1, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is a document which I think we generally refer to as the Sarajevo agreement, which is not by any means a final agreement. It was merely a -- as it says right at the end of it, a document to serve as the basis for further negotiations, but those are certainly the terms of that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, how come, Dr. Treanor, that these were not conditions? The first three items here say that this is what is to be negotiated. Those were the conditions. We can't start the negotiations every morning from square one like Izetbegovic did. Wasn't this an undertaking on our part that we would not secede and join other states in item 2?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. I don't read that document as an undertaking. These again are the bases for further negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, Izetbegovic didn't think it was a condition either and then the war broke out. Do you see that Serbs and Croats and Muslims have sovereignty and they will realise it through their civic participation in the constituent units?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I think this was regarded by Bosnian Serb leaders, including Dr. Karadzic, as being the most important aspect of these negotiations, the most important victory that they won during these negotiations was to gain the recognition by their negotiating partners and indeed the international community, that Bosnia and Herzegovina could be divided along ethnic lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll see tomorrow who celebrated that, if Serbs were the only one.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we just see page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting, Doctor, the Muslim side also proclaimed it their victory, and we will show that tomorrow. Did you know that Ajanovic had stated that it was a victory for the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I -- well, I think I have read some of his statements at that time. Of course, at this time the Bosnian Muslim leaders -- or shortly after the date of this document they, and I think the Croats as well, started to back off of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid you mixed up these two things. It was the Muslims who reneged seven days later. Do you agree it would have been Serbian victory if Bosnia had remained within Yugoslavia or if Serbian lands had remained Yugoslavia, that would have been victory for us? This, instead, was a very painful blow.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that's what I said, that the Muslims as well as the Croats backed off of their acceptance of this document -- well, yes, that's what the Serbs were hoping to achieve, that is, remaining in Yugoslavia. And indeed at this time I would remind the Court that in March 1992, Bosnia still was technically part of Yugoslavia. We saw during my direct examination that around this time, as a voice during the meeting in Belgrade that Dr. Karadzic attended at the beginning of March, that it seemed to be the Serbian view that Bosnia would remain in -- within Yugoslavia as long as the negotiations continued and that the JNA would remain in the Serbian portions of Bosnia as long as Bosnia remained within Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Treanor, if we had more time we would have shed light on all that, but I'm asking you now to look at section D, constituencies. Do you agree that this agreement stipulates that constituent units would have their Assemblies, government, executive power, legislative power? Do you agree that this envisages that Bosnian constituent units would have something not unlike what the republics had in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how you want to qualify a comparison between these units and the units within Yugoslavia, but that portion of the document certainly does deal with those issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have the next page, page 3, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 3, Article 2 [as interpreted] says: [In English] "Members of the nations who would be in a minority in a particular constituent unit would receive protection similar to that in Article 2(3) of the draft Convention." [Interpretation] Do you know and do you agree that we accepted this document, we adopted it with all its articles without any reservations to any of the articles?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that all three parties accepted this document as the basis for further negotiations on that date, the 18th of March, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did then the Serbs accept having part of them living in constituent units of the Muslims and Croats and a part of the Muslims and Croats live in a Serbian constituent unit and that they would enjoy all rights, the protection of their rights?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That seems to be the -- one of the terms of this document, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, in your report on page 4, in conclusion E2, you state the following -- actually, it's document 592: [In English] "Through the party-derived structures under their influence or control, the Bosnian Serb leadership directed the political and administrative processes which eventually enabled the Bosnian Serbs to secure control of territories and led to large-scale ethnic cleansing of non-Serbs in those territories in spring 1992 ..."

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you agree that on the 18th of March, we devoted to respecting what was agreed, that the national minorities would exist and that there would be mutual protection of their rights?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Again, those are the terms of that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you know or did you come across me saying, after returning from Brussels on the 3rd of May, 1992, in response to a question from a journalist whether it was envisaged that the population be transferred, I said, "No, we do not envisage that or recommend the transference of the population." Just yes or no, did you take this into account, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't specifically recall that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you look at section E, definition of the constituent units. [In English] "A working group will be established in order to define the territory of the constituent units based on national principles and taking into account economic, geographical, and other criteria. A map based on the national absolute or relative majority in each municipality will be the basis of work in the working group, and will be subject only to amendments, justified by the above-mentioned criteria. A copy is annexed to this Statement." [Interpretation] But you see, Doctor, that the principles were agreed upon and that we were moving forward. What was for negotiation was not principles but maps, the aspect of the units themselves, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the negotiations were moving forward at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And on page 5 of that same document, a map is attached of the ethnic division of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it is D91 for us to look at on e-court. This is not quite an original, but it does say Carrington-Cutileiro. It's been somewhat modified, but do you agree there is no continuity here, neither of the Serb, Muslim, or Croat territories, that the territory has been discontinued of the constituent units?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: But let me just say that this map, the Cutileiro map, whether this is it or not I don't know, it seems to be, is simply a map that showed the relative ethnic majority in each municipality, presumably on the basis of the 1991 census. That's what this looks like. And the Court can see what here are described as cantons which, I think, is a term not used in the document we were looking at. I think they were referred to as constituent units. Are not -- the cantons of the three peoples are not all contiguous.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't see. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just to -- first of all, wondering if the Defence could identify all the ways that this document has been modified and perhaps indicate to us the reason for using a modified document in the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you help us, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we didn't modify it. 1D00 -- and the number there. We downloaded it. The original document was written -- was drawn by hand, 782, page 4, the previous document, please. It's similar. This is just technically more sophisticated. I just brought it up so that we could see that it was accepted that three constituent units didn't mean territorial unit -- continuity. Contiguity. This is the original document. Can we turn it around?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The previous map allegedly modified, Mr. Tieger, was it not one that was already admitted as -- into evidence, D --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I can't say offhand, Your Honour, but we'll certainly check immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's D91. But as such -- we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Treanor, would you please look and see if you agree that what was -- that this is the hand-drawn map as a component part of the agreement and that the other one we showed was just more sophisticated in technical terms, more perfect in technical terms, but that this is the hand-drawn map?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I certainly recognise the hand-drawn map. I would have to -- as the Court can see, it's not very user-friendly. And I would have to examine it and the other map side by side in some detail to see whether it's -- the modified map is accurate in that respect, but in general terms it seems to be. Again, this is a map that shows the relative majorities of the three principal peoples in Bosnia-Herzegovina by municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We have time to look at D302 to see how enthusiastic we all were about avoiding a war. D302 to see how high-ranking official of the Party of Democratic Action, a deputy in the Federal Republic of -- federal Assembly of Yugoslavia, Irfan Ajanovic, comments on the agreement reached.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we see the highlighted portion and then the translation of that highlighted portion on the second half of the screen. And we need the translation as well. The title is: "Reactions in the SDA to the fifth round on Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Muslims are satisfied with the statehood agreed." And now can we zoom in to the Serbian. Thank you. It says: "That he commented and as the porte-parole spokesperson he said that the Muslim nation in its constituent unit or future ethnic canton would be a majority of 82 per cent represented, while the Serbian people would comprise only 50 per cent ..." And he goes on to list the advantages of the agreement and that the Muslim side fared well in the agreement as did Croatia, if a little less so, whereas the Serbian side fared worst, came out of it worse. And now may we have D303 displayed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Karadzic, it is time to rise for us. Could you put a question and finish for today.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thought it was part of the same question. May we just take one minute to look at 303?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Treanor, "The SDA to renounce the Sarajevo agreement." And that was the 26th of March, from the 18th to the 26th of March. "After all the jubilation and celebration that was held, the SDA renounces the agreement that we had already reached ..." Did you note and underline and stress in your report that the agreement was reached and needed to be further elaborated but that one week later the SDA pulled out, renounced it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that is in the report. I believe I mentioned the fact that both agreements, the so-called Lisbon Agreement in February and the Sarajevo Agreement in March were both later rejected by the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On that same page it says that the -- a thousand shells from Croatia fell on Bosanski Brod. Did you know that we were negotiating and that political life was evolving under a spray of shells falling from Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we zoom in to the Serbian. Zoom out, please. Sorry, zoom out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Believe me when I say that it says here: "A thousand shells have so far fallen on Bosanski Brod ..." Did you know that that's how life was? And it goes on to say that shells fell on Derventa too.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware that that was happening at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll have that portion translated as well, from the paper "Politika," with the Trial Chamber's permission. And with that I have completed my examination for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I wanted to note that this document referred to as D303 is the one that has not been admitted, that was denied, that's marked as not admitted. You tender -- you used it with Dr. Donia, but I -- the e-court says it was never admitted. But we'll continue tomorrow. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I just wanted to mention, Your Honour, the scheduling proposal --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- for later this month is -- we don't see any problem with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So instead of 16th, we'll be sitting on 24th, Friday --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's as we understood it and we didn't identify any --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we adopt the document -- admit it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Likewise, in the case of Mr. Donia, I don't think there's a basis for us to admit this with this witness. We'll continue tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But he confirmed it, Your Excellency, he confirmed that he knows they were first happy about it and then they reneged on it, both documents confirm it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's deal with it tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 8th day of June, 2011, at 9.00 a.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
